title: The Blind Man and the Lame Man in the Orchard
text:
The Talmud records a conversation between the Roman Antoninus and Rabbi Judah the Prince. Antoninus argued that body and soul could each escape judgment. The body could say that it was the soul that sinned, since once the soul left, the body lay still like a stone. The soul could say that it was the body that sinned, since without the body it flew through the air like a bird.

Rabbi Judah answered with a parable. A king had a beautiful orchard with fine early figs. He set two watchmen to guard it, one lame and one blind. The lame man said to the blind man that he could see wonderful figs in the orchard. Come, he said, let me ride on your shoulders and we will get them and eat them. The blind man carried the lame man, and together they picked the figs and ate them.

Some time later the king came and asked where his figs had gone. The lame man said: do I have legs to walk to them? The blind man said: do I have eyes to see them? So the king set the lame man on the blind man's shoulders and judged them as one. In the same way, Rabbi Judah said, God puts the soul back into the body and judges them together.
lesson: When partners achieve something together, they share responsibility for it together. Neither can claim the gain and then blame the other for the harm.
